patch.objective: Encrypting data at rest with AWS KMS, and writing key policies that hold

sources.cite: AWS Certified Solutions Architect - Associate (SAA-C03) exam guide (PDF): Design Secure Architectures 30%, Design Resilient Architectures 26%, Design High-Performing Architectures 24%, Design Cost-Optimized Architectures 20%
sources.note: Read through a summarizing fetch of the PDF on 2026-11-17. Quoted: Task 2.1 'Determining the AWS services required to achieve loose coupling based on requirements', Task 3.2 'Decoupling workloads so that components can scale independently'; Task 1.3 'Encrypting data at rest (for example, AWS KMS)', 'Implementing access policies for encryption keys'; Task 2.2 'Service quotas and throttling', Task 4.4 'Selecting an appropriate throttling strategy'.

sources.cite: AWS KMS Developer Guide, Allowing users in other accounts to use a KMS key
sources.note: Read through a summarizing fetch on 2026-11-17. Quoted: 'Neither the key policy nor the IAM policy alone is sufficient - you must change both'; the key policy in the owning account must give the external account (or its roles) permission; IAM policies in the external account delegate it, and can only grant actions the key policy also allows. The KMS guide (read 2026-11-18): 'AWS KMS retains all key material for a KMS key ... AWS KMS deletes key material only when you delete the KMS key', and decryption automatically uses the version that encrypted the data (rotate-keys.html); 'You cannot change the key policies of AWS managed keys' (key-policy-modifying.html).
